sections.title: Carbohydrates and lipids: structure, types and biological role
Proteins and enzymes: structure, types and biological role

summary: Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones; glucose is an aldohexose, fructose a ketohexose, ribulose a ketopentose.
Sucrose (glucose + fructose, α-1 → β-2) is non-reducing; maltose, lactose and cellobiose are reducing.
Starch (amylose + amylopectin) and glycogen are α-glucose stores with α-1,4 chains and α-1,6 branches; cellulose is β-1,4 glucose; chitin is β-1,4 N-acetylglucosamine; inulin is a fructose polymer.
A triglyceride is glycerol esterified with three fatty acids (three water molecules lost); lipids give about 39 kJ g⁻¹, more than twice carbohydrate.
Phospholipids are amphipathic and form membrane bilayers; steroids have four fused rings; waxes are esters of long-chain alcohols.

Seventeen elements are essential; Mg is in chlorophyll, Mo in nitrogenase, Mn and Cl split water, Ca forms calcium pectate, Zn is needed for auxin; mobile N, P, K, Mg show deficiency in old leaves first.

Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds (n − 1 for n residues); secondary structure is held by H-bonds, tertiary adds ionic, disulphide and hydrophobic bonds, quaternary needs two or more chains.
Enzymes lower activation energy; holoenzyme = apoenzyme + cofactor; the induced-fit model (Koshland) replaced lock-and-key (Fischer).

sections.title: Classification systems, taxonomic hierarchy and binomial nomenclature

summary: Linnaeus (1758) gave two kingdoms; Whittaker (1969) gave five — Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia — chiefly on cell structure, body organisation and mode of nutrition; Woese (1990) placed three domains — Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya — above them, on rRNA sequences.
The hierarchy runs kingdom, division, class, order (-ales), family (-aceae), genus, species; species is the basic unit.
Binomial names (Linnaeus, 1753): Latin, genus capitalised, epithet small, italicised or underlined separately; tautonyms are not allowed in plants.
Bacteria have a peptidoglycan wall, 70S ribosomes, a nucleoid and often plasmids; they are cocci, bacilli, vibrios or spirilla.
Gram-positive walls have thick peptidoglycan and stay violet; Gram-negative walls are thin with an outer lipopolysaccharide membrane and stain pink.
Bacteria are photoautotrophic (anoxygenic, except cyanobacteria), chemoautotrophic (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter), saprophytic, parasitic or symbiotic.
Binary fission doubles the population each generation (N = N0 × 2^n); the growth curve has lag, log, stationary and decline phases.
Cyanobacteria are oxygenic prokaryotes with chlorophyll a and phycobilins, cyanophycean starch, heterocysts for N₂ fixation, and no flagella or sexual reproduction.

sections.title: Fungi: the four classes; yeast and Mucor
Algae: green, red and brown; Spirogyra

summary: Fungi are eukaryotic, achlorophyllous absorptive heterotrophs with chitin walls and glycogen and oil as food; their sexual cycle is plasmogamy, karyogamy, meiosis.

Phycomycetes have coenocytic hyphae and zygospores or oospores; Ascomycetes form 8 endogenous ascospores in an ascus; Basidiomycetes form 4 exogenous basidiospores on a basidium; Deuteromycetes have no known sexual stage.
Phytophthora (late blight), Albugo (white rust), Claviceps (ergot), Puccinia (rust), Ustilago (smut), Alternaria (early blight) and Colletotrichum (red rot) are the classic disease fungi.
Yeast is a unicellular ascomycete that buds, ferments sugar with zymase to ethanol and CO₂, and forms 4 ascospores; its cycle is haplo-diplontic.
Mucor has a coenocytic mycelium without rhizoids, sporangia with a columella, heterothallic conjugation and a zygospore that is its only diploid stage.
A lichen is a fungus (mycobiont) living with an alga or cyanobacterium (phycobiont); its forms are crustose, foliose and fruticose, and it spreads by soredia and isidia.
Lichens are pioneers on bare rock and sensitive indicators of SO₂ pollution.

Green algae store starch and have chl a, b; brown algae store laminarin and mannitol and have fucoxanthin and algin; red algae store floridean starch, have phycoerythrin and agar, and never have flagella.

sections.title: Bryophytes: liverworts, hornworts and mosses; Marchantia

summary: Bryophytes are non-vascular embryophytes with a dominant haploid gametophyte and a dependent diploid sporophyte; water is needed for their biflagellate sperm.

Liverworts (thalloid, unicellular rhizoids, scales, elaters), hornworts (horn-like capsule, one chloroplast per cell) and mosses (leafy, multicellular rhizoids, protonema, peristome) are the three classes.

Marchantia is a dioecious, dichotomous thallus with barrel-shaped air pores and gemma cups; it bears stalked antheridiophores and archegoniophores; its capsule holds haploid spores and diploid elaters.
Pteridophytes are the first vascular plants; their dominant sporophyte has roots, stems and leaves; most are homosporous, but Selaginella, Marsilea, Salvinia and Azolla are heterosporous.

Dryopteris has a rhizome with ramenta, circinate fronds, and sori with a reniform indusium; its sporangium opens by the annulus; the spore grows into a free-living, heart-shaped, protandrous prothallus; sperm are multiflagellate.
Gymnosperms bear naked ovules, are wind-pollinated, have a haploid endosperm formed before fertilisation and no double fertilisation, and lack vessels and fruits.

Pinus is monoecious with long and dwarf shoots, needles in fascicles, winged pollen, and two ovules on each ovuliferous scale; fertilisation follows pollination by about a year; polyembryony is common.
A Pinus seed holds three generations: seed coat 2n, endosperm n, embryo 2n.

sections.title: Morphology of root, stem, leaf, inflorescence, flower and fruit
Economic importance of plant groups in Nepal
Medicinal plants of Nepal: neem, sarpagandha, yarsagumba, tulasi and ginger

summary: A modified organ is identified by its origin, not its looks: nodes, buds or scale leaves mean stem (potato, ginger, onion, Colocasia, Opuntia pad, Asparagus cladode, Citrus thorn); sweet potato, carrot and radish are roots; pea tendrils and Opuntia spines are leaves.

Racemose inflorescences grow on and open acropetally; cymose ones end in a flower and open basipetally; tulasi has a verticillaster, Euphorbia a cyathium, the fig a hypanthodium and the sunflower a capitulum.

Flower terms the paper uses: actinomorphic or zygomorphic; hypo-, peri- or epigynous; valvate, twisted, imbricate or vexillary aestivation; monadelphous, diadelphous, syngenesious, epipetalous, tetradynamous and didynamous stamens.
Placentation is marginal (pea), axile (tomato, lily), parietal (mustard), free central (Dianthus) or basal (sunflower).
Fruits are simple, aggregate (many free carpels of one flower) or composite (a whole inflorescence); false fruits such as the apple include the thalamus.

Brassicaceae: Ebr ⊕ ⚥ K₂₊₂ C₄ A₂₊₄ G₍₂₎, siliqua. Fabaceae: Br % ⚥ K₍₅₎ C₁₊₂₊₍₂₎ A₍₉₎₊₁ G₁, legume. Solanaceae: ⊕ ⚥ K₍₅₎ C₍₅₎ A₅ G₍₂₎ with epipetalous stamens and an oblique ovary, berry. Liliaceae: Br ⊕ ⚥ P₃₊₃ A₃₊₃ G₍₃₎, capsule.

Every group matters in Nepal: nitrogen-fixing bacteria and blue-green algae, gundruk and kinema, mushrooms and yeast, agar, Sphagnum, Azolla, pine resin and timber, taxol, lokta paper and sal timber — and the harm done by plant viruses, late blight, aflatoxin, poisonous mushrooms and invasive weeds.

The five named medicinal plants: neem (Azadirachta indica, azadirachtin), sarpagandha (Rauwolfia serpentina, reserpine, roots), yarsagumba (Ophiocordyceps sinensis, an ascomycete on ghost-moth larvae, cordycepin), tulasi (Ocimum sanctum, eugenol, leaves) and ginger (Zingiber officinale, rhizome, gingerols).
